H1.text: Throw a ball straight up. It passes fifteen metres twice, once going up and once coming down.

H2.text: It reaches twenty metres only once, right at the top. And twenty five metres? Never.

H3.text: Aarav tried this on his way home from college today.

H4.text: Every height gives the same kind of equation. So why two answers, then one, then none?

H5.text: Here is the twist. Even never has two answers. They just do not live on the number line.

P1.text: Each height question is a quadratic equation.

P2.text: A quadratic equation looks like this. a x squared, plus b x, plus c, equals zero, and a is not zero.

P3.text: a, b and c are fixed numbers, called the coefficients. The values of x that make it true are called its roots.

P4.text: For the ball, we take the height as twenty t minus five t squared. Height fifteen means this equals fifteen.

P5.text: Move everything to one side and divide by five. We get t squared minus four t plus three equals zero.

P6.text: It factors into t minus one, times t minus three. So t is one second going up, or three seconds coming down.

L1.text: Now watch the whole family at once. Here is y equals x squared minus four x plus c. For the ball, c is the height divided by five.

L2.text: The roots are where the curve meets the x axis. Let c count up.

L3.text: At c equals zero, the roots are zero and four. As c grows, the curve lifts, and the roots slide towards each other.

L4.text: At c equals four, they meet at two. The curve just touches the axis. The two roots are equal.

L5.text: Past four, the curve leaves the axis. No real root is left. But look at the map on the right.

L6.text: The two roots have stepped off the number line, one up and one down. At c equals five, they are two plus i and two minus i.

L7.text: Quick one. At c equals six, are the roots real or complex? Pause and think.

L8.text: Complex! Past four the curve stays above the axis. The roots are two plus i root two, and two minus i root two.

D1.text: Where do those roots come from? Let us build one formula that works for every quadratic.

D2.text: Step one. Divide everything by a, so x squared stands alone.

D3.text: Step two. Move c over a to the right side.

D4.text: Step three. Add b over two a, squared, to both sides. Now the left side is a perfect square.

D5.text: Step four. Take the square root of both sides. Plus or minus, because both signs give the same square.

D6.text: Step five. Subtract b over two a. This is the quadratic formula.

D7.text: On the curve, minus b over two a is the middle line. The roots sit at equal distances on either side of it.

D8.text: Now, if b squared minus four a c is negative, its square root is not real. But the square root of minus one is i. So the root becomes i times a real number, and the formula still works.

S1.text: Side by side. x squared minus four x plus three. The curve crosses the axis twice. The roots are one and three, both real.

S2.text: x squared minus four x plus five. The curve never touches the axis. Under the root we get minus four, so the roots are two plus i and two minus i.

S3.text: Notice the pair. Same real part, opposite imaginary parts. These are conjugates. When a, b and c are real, complex roots always come as a conjugate pair.

K1.text: Your turn. Does x squared plus nine equal zero have real roots? Pause and decide.

K2.text: No! x squared would have to be minus nine, and no real number squares to a negative. The roots are three i and minus three i.

T1.text: Remember this. Every quadratic equation has two roots. Real or complex, one formula finds them both.

W2.text: Solve x squared plus x plus one equals zero.

W3.text: Step one. Here a, b and c are all one.

W4.text: Step two. b squared minus four a c is one minus four, which is minus three.

W5.text: Step three. The square root of minus three is i root three.

W6.text: Step four. So x is minus one, plus or minus i root three, all over two.

W7.text: Two complex roots, a conjugate pair, both with real part minus one half.

X2.text: Solve x squared minus two x plus five equals zero. Under the root we get minus sixteen. Many students write its square root as minus four, and get three and minus one.

X3.text: But the square root of minus sixteen is four i, not minus four. Check: three does not even fit the equation. The roots are one plus two i, and one minus two i.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as questions where you first solve a quadratic with complex roots, then use those roots, like the April twenty nineteen paper. It is in the JEE Main syllabus, but not in the current NCERT text.

Q1.text: Exam level now. The two roots of this equation and the origin make a triangle on the Argand plane. Find its area. Pause and solve.

A2.text: b squared minus four a c is sixteen minus fifty two, which is minus thirty six.

A3.text: Its square root is six i. So x is four plus or minus six i, over two. That is two plus three i, and two minus three i.

A4.text: Both roots sit above and below the point two. The base is six, and its distance from the origin is two. Half of six times two is six.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Solve x squared plus four equals zero.

Y3.text: Two. Why does the formula need plus or minus?

Y4.text: Three. Three minus two i is a root of a quadratic with real coefficients. What is the other root?

N1.text: Next time: one small number tells you if the roots are real, equal or complex, before you solve anything. It is called the discriminant.
